cited_by.title: Colourism, skin tone and mental health

record.population: Clients and therapists across 52 to 81 studies per question; countries not stated in the abstract
record.finding: Matching made almost no difference to treatment outcomes on average (d 0.09), despite a moderately strong preference for a matched therapist (d 0.63). Studies with African American participants had the highest effect sizes.

cited_by.title: Finding a Black therapist or one who understands being Black

record.population: Clients and therapists across 52 to 81 studies per question; countries not stated in the abstract
record.design: Meta-analysis of racial/ethnic matching: preferences, perceptions and outcomes
record.finding: People preferred a therapist of their own race or ethnicity (d 0.63, moderately strong) and rated them somewhat more positively (d 0.32), but matching made almost no difference to treatment outcomes on average (d 0.09). Effects varied a lot between studies, and studies with African American participants had the highest effect sizes on all three.
record.note: Abstract read in full. Mostly US data; the abstract does not say how many studies were UK (UNVERIFIED).
